quizzes.title: Why Austerity Is Sought (MCQ)
quizzes.passage: India's foreign exchange reserves have fallen sharply within a short period. The booklet describes a drop of nearly USD 38 billion over two months, taking the reserves to around USD 691 billion by May 2026. The decline has been linked to volatile oil prices, record-breaking gold imports and the central bank's market intervention to defend the rupee. In response to growing concerns over the reserves, the Prime Minister has urged citizens to reduce non-essential spending on gold purchases, overseas travel and fuel. The government's concern is that the current account deficit has widened at a time when the currency is under pressure. Household gold imports, in particular, do not add to productive capacity. Rising fertiliser prices have added another layer to the problem, forcing a choice between fuel use and food security, and the government has given food security the higher priority. The booklet says the strategy must balance the immediate need for financial security against the long-term health of the nation's industrial sectors. The booklet presents these steps as part of a wider effort aimed at the economy's future needs. The measures are meant to provide currency stability and manage inflation. The booklet frames these concerns as central to the government's current approach.

questions.q: According to the booklet, how much does each USD 1 increase in the price of oil add to India's import bill?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that every USD 1 increase in oil price adds USD 1.5 to 2 billion to the import bill.

questions.q: Which feature of import demand does the booklet cite as a reason for a persistent current account deficit?
questions.explanation: The booklet attributes the persistent current account deficit to inelastic import demand and increased dependence on external financing.

questions.q: What does the booklet identify as the implication of declining forex reserves?
options: Lower sensitivity to global capital flows
A surplus in the balance of payments
Higher gold reserves held by the RBI
questions.explanation: The booklet says lower reserves mean a reduced buffer against external shocks and higher sensitivity to global capital flow fluctuations.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cutting non-essential imports helps India conserve foreign exchange.
Reason (R): Foreign exchange reserves are external assets maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
questions.explanation: Both statements appear in the booklet, but the fact that reserves are RBI-maintained assets does not explain why cutting imports conserves forex.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Demand-side behavioural measures   ->   A. Work-from-home adoption, carpooling and virtual meetings
II. Gold imports in FY26   ->   B. Rose by nearly 25% to USD 71.97 billion
III. Strategic autonomy   ->   C. Shift from supply-side diversification to demand-side restraint
IV. Containing capital flight   ->   D. Reducing foreign exchange outflows
questions.explanation: The booklet links work-from-home and carpooling to demand-side measures, gold imports rose nearly 25% in FY26, strategic autonomy means the shift to demand-side restraint, and capital flight containment reduces forex outflows.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the goals behind the shift to demand-side restraint:
I. Lowering energy-to-GDP sensitivity is one of the stated goals.
II. Increasing dependence on volatile regions is one of the stated goals.
III. Strengthening resilience against global shocks is one of the stated goals.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists reducing, not increasing, dependence on volatile regions as a goal, so only statements I and III are correct.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements on the import bill and the rupee are correct?
I. Energy imports form one part of India's twin import burden.
II. Non-essential imports are excluded from India's twin import burden.
III. A weaker rupee raises the cost of imports.
IV. Sharp increases in imports can lead to a reduction in forex reserves.
questions.explanation: Statements I, III and IV match the booklet, while statement II reverses the twin import burden, which includes non-essential imports.

quizzes.title: Why Austerity Is Sought (TITA)
quizzes.passage: India's foreign exchange reserves have declined in recent months, and the government has responded by asking citizens to spend less on certain items. The Prime Minister has urged people to limit discretionary spending on gold purchases, overseas travel and fuel. Gold imports have reached record levels, and the booklet notes that household gold purchases do not add to the country's productive capacity. Fuel is another pressure point, since oil prices feed directly into the import bill and into the cost of living. The booklet also explains that the government has had to weigh fuel use against food security because of rising fertiliser costs. The booklet notes that a weaker rupee makes imports more expensive, which in turn pushes up domestic prices. Restraint is also meant to limit capital leaving the country and to keep the rupee steady. The booklet describes the broader purpose as making India's economy better prepared for unexpected developments abroad and less dependent on certain regions for its energy. The steps are also described as a way to lower the country's exposure to changes in energy costs. Each of these pressures has to be weighed against the others. Such steps are presented as a way to balance short-term financial needs with the long-term health of the economy.

questions.q: By how many billion US dollars does each USD 1 rise in the price of oil add to India's import bill, at the lower end of the booklet's range? (number, in billion USD)
questions.explanation: The booklet says every USD 1 increase in oil price adds USD 1.5 to 2 billion to the import bill.

questions.q: By roughly what percentage did gold imports rise in FY26? (number, in per cent)
questions.explanation: The booklet says gold imports in FY26 jumped by nearly 25% to USD 71.97 billion.

questions.q: What term does the booklet use for the approach that shifts from supply-side diversification to demand-side restraint? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet's heading 'Enhancing Strategic Autonomy' describes this shift in approach.

questions.q: Which demand-side measure, in which employees work remotely, does the booklet suggest to reduce fuel use? (name it in two or three words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists work-from-home adoption among the demand-side measures to reduce fuel consumption.

questions.q: The policy aims to reduce dependence on which type of regions? (one word)
questions.explanation: One stated goal is to reduce dependence on volatile regions.

questions.q: Apart from energy imports, what is the other component of India's twin import burden? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet describes the twin import burden as energy imports and non-essential imports.

questions.q: Declining forex reserves reduce the buffer against which type of events? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says lower reserves mean a reduced buffer against external shocks.

quizzes.title: Costs of Excessive Forex Conservation (MCQ)
quizzes.passage: The booklet argues that the drive to conserve foreign exchange carries costs for the wider economy. It cautions that overly strict controls could stifle manufacturing and broader economic growth. The text also looks back at history, and earlier efforts to reduce dependence on foreign goods are presented as a warning. Household spending is another concern, as the booklet examines how curbs on it would affect the wider economy. Industry is also in view. The booklet notes that a balance must be struck between the immediate need for financial security and the long-term health of industrial sectors. In this account, policymakers must weigh the value of stable reserves against the risks to manufacturing and growth. Measures taken to protect the currency therefore have to be judged against their effects on the wider economy. The booklet lists several channels through which these effects could spread, including manufacturing, household spending and the broader growth of the economy. The booklet also places this discussion within the current concerns about the rupee and the reserves, which have been under pressure in recent months. The text also states that imports become more expensive when the rupee weakens. This linkage is part of the wider picture the booklet paints for the economy.

questions.q: According to the booklet, what is the effect of restricting imports on the economy?
questions.explanation: The booklet says restricted imports lower industrial output and exports.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Reducing private consumption strengthens economic growth.
Reason (R): Private consumption is a major component of GDP.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The booklet says reducing private consumption weakens growth, so A is false while R is a true statement from the booklet.

questions.q: What does the booklet say Indian industry depends on imports for?
options: Imported capital goods, semiconductors and raw materials
Agricultural produce such as wheat and rice
questions.explanation: The booklet states that Indian industry depends on imported capital goods, semiconductors and raw materials.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Lower production activity   ->   A. Significantly reduced job creation
II. Past import-substitution efforts   ->   B. Low industrial competitiveness and inefficiency
III. Capital control concerns   ->   C. Raise the country risk premium
IV. Weak consumer spending   ->   D. Businesses avoid fresh investment and expansion
questions.explanation: Each pair matches a cause with its consequence as stated in the booklet's section on the risks of suppressing consumption.

questions.q: How do foreign investors respond to economies lacking strong domestic demand and high growth potential?
options: They shift only to government bonds
questions.explanation: The booklet says foreign investors avoid economies lacking strong domestic demand and high growth potential.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the costs of strict import curbs:
I. Foreign direct and portfolio investment inflows could be dampened.
II. Restricted imports raise industrial output.
III. Suppressing consumption mirrors past strategies that led to slower-than-expected economic development.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The booklet says investment inflows could be dampened and that suppressing consumption mirrors past slow-growth strategies, while restricted imports lower rather than raise output.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the costs of forex conservation are correct?
I. Suppressing private consumption threatens aggregate demand.
II. Excessive forex conservation has no effect on investment inflows.
III. Past import-substitution attempts led to high industrial competitiveness.
IV. Capital control concerns lower the country risk premium.
questions.explanation: Only statement I matches the booklet, since the booklet says investment inflows could be dampened and past import substitution caused low competitiveness.

quizzes.title: Costs of Excessive Forex Conservation (TITA)
quizzes.passage: The booklet warns that tight control over foreign exchange can have side effects on growth. It says that overly strict controls could stifle manufacturing and broader economic growth, and that Indian industry relies on inputs from abroad for production. Curbing those inputs could reduce output across factories. Capital controls may also change how outsiders view the country, which can hold back the money that would otherwise come in. The booklet points to a past approach as a cautionary example: earlier efforts to cut dependence on foreign goods are said to have resulted in weak industrial performance. Consumption is another channel of concern. Curbs on household spending are seen as a risk to economic growth. Lower production has wider consequences across sectors, and the booklet also warns that a slowdown can weaken the overall economy. The balance, it concludes, must be struck between immediate financial security and the long-term health of industry. The booklet frames these choices as trade-offs that must be made carefully. The booklet's examples come from the current debate over the reserves, which fell to around USD 691 billion by May 2026. Reserves, rupee stability and the cost of imports all feature in this argument. The text also states that imports become more expensive when the rupee weakens.

questions.q: Capital control concerns raise which premium on the country? (three words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says capital control concerns raise the country risk premium, which can dampen investment inflows.

questions.q: Along with FDI, which other type of foreign investment inflow could be dampened? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says both foreign direct and portfolio investment inflows could be dampened.

questions.q: What is the name of the past strategy the booklet cites as producing low industrial competitiveness? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says past import-substitution efforts led to low industrial competitiveness and inefficiency.

questions.q: Lower production leads to significantly reduced what? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says lower production leads to significantly reduced job creation.

questions.q: Restricted imports lower industrial output and which other variable? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet says restricted imports lower both industrial output and exports.

questions.q: Foreign investors avoid economies lacking strong what? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet says foreign investors avoid economies lacking strong domestic demand and high growth potential.

questions.q: Suppressing private consumption threatens which economic aggregate? (two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists a threat to aggregate demand as one of the risks of suppressing consumption.
